Q: PostgreSQL: Will DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED prevent this race condition? A:

If not isolation level and/or deferrability, what else could help?
(not a quote, I'm just assuming this should naturally follow)

You could start T2 by acquiring a row lock in B, on the thing you're referencing from A:

select from b where id=$1
for key share of b /*nowait*/;
  • If there's a conflicting T1 in progress, T2 waits at that initial statement and regardless of whether that row ends up updated, reinserted, deleted, once it gets the lock, T2 can proceed to safely run the vulnerable insert, now without the risk of waiting for a disappearing row caused by the concurrent reinsert.
  • If a T1 appears while T2 is in progress, it's T1 that will have to wait for the lock held by T2.

As clarified in the comments under @Laurenz Albe's post, this technically still leaves a window of opportunity for another, new T1 to sneak in between T2's initial locking select and the insert that's supposed to fire immediately after it. That's because after a successful reinsert in T1, the select in T2 only saves the insert from the bait-and-switch, but it doesn't secure an actual lock on anything - it just gracefully accepts the original row's gone and lets the update do the whole constraint check again, safely.

That can be solved by chaining these two not as separate statements, but as a single atomic, two-part operation, using a CTE:

with cte as (select from b 
             where id=1 
             for key share /*nowait*/ )
insert into a select payload.* 
from (values(1,1)) as payload
left join cte on true
limit 1;--avoids multiplying the payload if cte manages to lock many rows

The join is necessary to convince the planner that the main, outer query relies on the completion of what's in the CTE - the select needs to have already taken the incoming shots before we let the insert begin and safely re-check the constraint.

You can uncomment nowait and use it to implement similar retry logic to the one mentioned by Laurenz' answer - it'll cause T2 to fail if a conflicting T1 is in progress. That could also be helpful if T1 has to be prioritised over T2 and for some reason you cannot afford introducing a lag in T1.

This example is also a reminder that for row-locking selects, exists() conditions and a few other things, you can have an empty select list.

If I declare the foreign key as DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, then the foreign key will be evaluated by T2 only when it commits, and the new row should be in B by that time. So, do I understand correctly it will help?

I don't think it would help. It doesn't affect how and what gets locked, only when - it will do the same "lookup->request row lock->wait->acquire->realise the row is gone" thing, just at a later time.

It might help only if the relative timing of T1 and T2 is somehow coupled, synced or coordinated, in a way that lets you trust that postponing T2's check gives just enough time, every time, for T1 to complete before T2's referential integrity check comes knocking.

If you're trying to nudge the timing, just making it deferrable could already shift things around even if it's initially immediate - that pushes things back from mid-statement to post-statement. Here you can find some more details on why immediate can actually end up the 2nd most immediate constraint check, non-deferrables being more or really immediate:

  • Why does PostgreSQL check a DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE constraint after each statement?

But if the problem is with the isolation level, will changing it help, too? Will either? Will both? What is better?

Changing the isolation level will not side-step the problem or change anything in the locking behaviour at the root of your problem. Combining it with deferrability doesn't change things. You could only use it to accommodate the retry logic suggested in @Laurenz Albe's great answer.
